sentences.text: The holotype specimen TMP 1989.055.0047 was found in the Wapiti Formation in central Alberta and dates to the late Campanian, approximately 73.27 ± 0.25 million years ago.
The species is known from a right frontal bone, fourteen loose teeth, and several postcranial bones including a rear caudal vertebra, a second finger claw, and a foot sickle claw.
Fragmentary remains of Boreonykus were discovered in the 1980s at the Pipestone Creek site in central Alberta while excavating a bonebed of the ceratopsid Pachyrhinosaurus lakustai.
Remains initially attributed to Boreonykus were partly referred to Saurornitholestes sp. in 2001.
The genus name Boreonykus is a variation of "Boreonychus", meaning "northern claw".
The specific name certekorum honors the Certek company, which provided financial support for the excavations.
Boreonykus certekorum is the only known species of the extinct genus Boreonykus, a dromaeosaurid dinosaur.
Boreonykus was originally classified in the subfamily Velociraptorinae but was recovered within Dromaeosaurinae in 2021.
The suffix "onykus" in the name is confusing as it erroneously suggests a relationship to Alvarezsauridae.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Boreonykus as Dromaeosaurinae.
Boreonykus lived approximately 73 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America.
The time range for Boreonykus is recorded as Campanian to Campanian, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
